sharedText: baptize you with fire and with the Holy Ghost
reason: The Baptist's promise, with the two elements transposed, and the catalogue adjudicates it in this book at 3 Nephi 9:20, where the risen Christ first makes it and where the inversion is argued at length. “With the Holy Ghost, and with fire” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16, both of which put the Holy Ghost first; the Book of Mormon's order, “with fire and with the Holy Ghost”, occurs in no KJV verse at all and is this book's standing form. 3 Nephi 12:1-2 is the same speaker using his own formula three chapters later, which ADJUDICATING §4 files here rather than as a second link. A reader who meets the phrase at 12:1 should be sent to 9:20.

sharedText: the meek shall inherit the earth
reason: The proposal is reasonable and the wording refuses it. Psalm 37:11 is the only Old Testament verse that holds the meek and the inheritance of the earth together — “But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace” — and it is the acknowledged background of Matthew 5:5. But “blessed are the meek” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is Matthew's. The psalm makes a prediction about a class; 3 Nephi 12:5 pronounces a blessing over them, in the beatitude form and in the beatitude's position between the mourners and the hungry. The link is at Matthew 5:5 with Psalm 37:11 recorded as its composite; this entry exists so that a reader who reaches for the psalm is told the catalogue reached for it too.

sharedText: a broken heart and a contrite spirit
reason: “Broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “contrite spirit” occurs in exactly two, so Psalm 34:18 is the only verse in the King James Bible holding both, and in the Book of Mormon's order — not Psalm 51:17, which readers reflexively name and which has the nouns crossed. That argument is made in full at 3 Nephi 9:20, where the same speaker first demands the sacrifice, and this verse is his own formula recurring within the same book eleven verses into a new discourse. Filed here under ADJUDICATING §4 with the reader sent to 9:20; the catalogue has also taken the pair to Psalm 34:18 at 2 Nephi 2:7, 2 Nephi 4:32 and Jacob 2:10.

Hardy's apparatus cross-references Exodus 20:13 and Deuteronomy 5:17 at this verse, and the catalogue records the sixth commandment as a composite of the link rather than as its source, because the mediation test is decisive against it. Exodus 20:13 and Deuteronomy 5:17 consist, in the KJV, of the four words “Thou shalt not kill” and nothing else. Every other word of 3 Nephi 12:21 — the frame “Ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time”, which occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all in Matthew 5, and the sanction “and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment”, whose central phrase occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both in Matthew 5 — is Matthew's. The Decalogue reaches this chapter through Matthew's quotation of it. The link is at Matthew 5:21.

Hardy cross-references Exodus 20:14 and Deuteronomy 5:18 here. On its own the verse cannot settle its own mediation — tools/mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence, because the commandment is worded identically in Exodus and in Matthew's quotation of it, and Deuteronomy's variant form (“Neither shalt thou commit adultery”) is the one the Book of Mormon does not have. The frame decides it: “by them of old time” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 5:21, 5:27 and 5:33, and in no Old Testament verse, and the Sermon at the Temple uses it at precisely those three points. A writer quoting the Decalogue directly would have no source for the phrase. The link is at Matthew 5:27.

Hardy cross-references Deuteronomy 24:1-4 here and the mediation test returns four decisive points against it. Deuteronomy has a long conditional about uncleanness found in a wife and instructs the husband to WRITE her a BILL of divorcement, give it in her hand and send her out of his house; 3 Nephi has none of the conditions, none of the delivery, and reads GIVE her a WRITING of divorcement. “Writing of divorcement” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 5:31 and Mark 10:4, and never in the Old Testament, which says “bill” in all three of its occurrences. The link is at Matthew 5:31.

Hardy cross-references Leviticus 19:12 and Numbers 30:2 here, and neither can be the source of the wording. Leviticus reads “ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God”; Numbers reads “he shall not break his word”. The Book of Mormon reads “Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths”, and “forswear” occurs in exactly one KJV verse in the whole Bible — Matthew 5:33. The mediation tool returns four decisive points for Matthew and none for either Old Testament candidate, including the connective “Again”. The link is at Matthew 5:33.

Isaiah 66:1 is where the throne and the footstool come from — “The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool” — and a reader working from the Old Testament will propose it. The possessive settles it in one syllable. Isaiah's oracle is spoken by God in the first person and reads “my footstool”; Matthew reports it about God and reads “his”, and “for it is his footstool” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has “his”. The mediation tool returns three decisive points for Matthew 5:34-35 and none for Isaiah, and the Book of Mormon also lacks every word of Isaiah's continuation about the house and the place of rest. Isaiah 66:1 is recorded as the composite of the links at 12:34 and 12:35.

sharedText: eye for eye, tooth for tooth
reason: Hardy cross-references Exodus 21:23-24, Leviticus 24:19-20 and Deuteronomy 19:21 here — the three King James statements of the talion — and all three are articleless: “eye for eye, tooth for tooth”, which occurs in exactly three KJV verses. Matthew alone writes “An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that is the Book of Mormon's form, articles and conjunction and all. Worth flagging for anyone re-running the check: tools/mediation-check.py reports the divergences as pointing both ways at this verse, because its aligner treats the stray indefinite articles as unmatched rather than as Matthean; the phrase count overturns that reading. The link is at Matthew 5:38.

Hardy cross-references Leviticus 19:18 here, and the verse's decisive half has no Old Testament source at all. Leviticus reads “thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD”; the Book of Mormon reads “thou shalt love thy neighbor, and hate thine enemy”, and “hate thine enemy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:43. No commandment to hate an enemy stands anywhere in the King James Old Testament, which is why Matthew's second clause has its own long literature. Whatever Matthew was quoting, what the Book of Mormon has is Matthew. The link is at Matthew 5:43.

reason: Hardy cross-references Matthew 5:46-47 at this verse, and the row records an absence rather than a borrowing: the Sermon at the Temple has no parallel to “For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same?” or to the salutation of brethren. There is not one shared distinctive word. The entry is written because the omission is the interesting fact — 3 Nephi 12:44-45 tracks Matthew 5:44-45 for fifty-seven words and 12:48 resumes at Matthew 5:48, so the gap is exactly two verses wide and exactly where the Judaean publicans stand. What fills it is 2 Corinthians 5:17, adjudicated as a link at 12:47. Hardy's pairing of the two references at one verse is the right pairing; this register separates them so that a reader is told which one is present and which is missing.

sharedText: (no parallel — the least commandments saying is absent)
reason: Matthew 5:19 — “Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven” — has no counterpart in the Sermon at the Temple, which runs straight from 12:18 (Matthew 5:18) to 12:20 (Matthew 5:20). Recorded because 12:20's replacement clause, “except ye shall keep my commandments, which I have commanded you at this time”, occupies the ground Matthew 5:19 covers and a reader may take it for a compressed rendering of that verse. It is not: nothing of Matthew 5:19's vocabulary survives — no breaking, no teaching, no least, no greatness — and the frame the Book of Mormon keeps (“except … ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven”) is verse 20's, whose closing eight words occur in exactly one KJV verse.

Offered by the n-gram stream against 12:29's “suffer none of these things to enter into your heart”, and it is the wrong direction of travel. Matthew 15:19 is about what comes OUT of the heart and defiles a man — “out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries” — while 3 Nephi 12:29 is a commandment about what must not be let IN. The two verses share the heart and a vice list and nothing else; the Sermon at the Temple's own list at 12:22-28 (anger, insult, lust) is Matthew 5's, not Matthew 15's, and 12:29 is a Book of Mormon summary of the sayings it has just quoted rather than a borrowing from elsewhere in the Gospel.

Luke 6:29 is the Synoptic parallel and it is not the source. Luke reads “unto him that smiteth thee on the one cheek offer also the other”; Matthew reads “whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also”, and “smite thee on thy right cheek” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has the right cheek, the verb “turn”, and Matthew's word order. The entry is filed as a class marker: at every point in this chapter where Matthew and Luke offer different wordings for the same saying — the cheek here, the coat and cloak at 12:40, the four commands of 12:44 — the Sermon at the Temple has Matthew's, and 12:41 reproduces a verse Luke does not contain at all.
